patients.summary: Young schoolteacher who joins in 2021 healthy apart from weekend binge drinking; PiZZ alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency with panacinar emphysema is found in 2023 and treated with weekly augmentation. A compressive radial palsy after a drinking night leaves radial tunnel pain, and two ED visits for cocaine intoxication follow while he denies use.

documents.title: New patient call
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Caller is a teacher in town, moved his care over from a practice he hasn't used in a few years. Wants a physical before the school year gets busy. No current meds per caller. Scheduled new patient physical 9/14 at 3:30 (after school). Membership paperwork and portal invite emailed. Asked him to bring any old records or vaccine card he has.

documents.title: New Patient Preventive Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
28-year-old man, middle school science teacher, new to us. Last saw a doctor several years ago for a sports physical type visit; no records coming. Feels well. Rides his bike to school most days when the weather allows, about 4 miles each way, no trouble with it.

PMH: none. PSH: none. Meds: none, no supplements. Allergies: no known drug allergies.

Family: father was diagnosed with emphysema at 42, he had smoked. Mother has cirrhosis that her doctors never found a cause for; she does not drink. One sister, healthy as far as he knows.

Social: single, lives alone in an apartment in Westfield. Has never smoked or vaped. Alcohol: little or nothing on school nights, but most weekends 6-8 drinks on a night out, sometimes both nights. AUDIT-C 6. Denies marijuana or other drugs.

ROS: negative for cough, wheeze, exertional symptoms, GI symptoms, mood symptoms. PHQ-2 0.

Exam: slim, well appearing. HEENT unremarkable. Neck supple, no thyroid enlargement. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear, good air movement. Abdomen soft, no liver edge or spleen felt. Skin clear. Neuro grossly normal.

A/P
1. Preventive: Tdap today (no record of one as an adult). Screening labs: CBC, CMP, lipids, one-time HIV and hep C. Flu shot when the clinic gets its supply.
2. Alcohol: talked about binge pattern and what counts as a standard drink. Suggested setting a weekend limit. He was receptive but feels it's mostly social. Revisit next year.
RTC 1 yr.

documents.title: Your lab results
documents.author: PCP

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Annual visit. Feels fine physically. Started his second year at the middle school.

Alcohol: this is the main thing. Weekend nights are now usually 8-10 drinks, sometimes starting Friday after work. He has tried twice this year to keep it to a few and ended up well past that. Called out sick one Monday in the spring after a long weekend and felt bad about it. A friend has said something to him. No morning drinking, no withdrawal shakes. AUDIT-C 8. Still denies other drugs.

No cough or wheeze. Still biking when he can. Weight down 2 kg from last year, he thinks from skipping meals on busy days.

Exam: thin, NAD. Heart RRR no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender, no hepatomegaly. No tremor.

A/P
1. Alcohol use disorder: drinking more than intended, failed attempts to cut down, missed work. Reviewed this directly with him. Offered a counselor referral and discussed that medication exists to help with cravings. He wants to try on his own first and does not want either right now. Agreed goal: no more than 4 drinks on any night, alcohol-free school nights. Will check in at visits.
2. Health maintenance: CBC, CMP today. Flu shot next month, nurse visit.
RTC 1 yr, sooner if he wants help with drinking.

orders.reason: progressive exertional dyspnea in a never smoker, father with early emphysema

documents.title: Office Visit: Shortness of Breath
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Gradually more short of breath with exertion over roughly the past year. Hills, then flats, now he stops partway on the bike and has quit commuting by bike because he arrives exhausted. Stairs at school fine at his own pace. Now and then a tight, uncomfortable feeling in the middle of the chest when pushing hard on the bike or running for the bus, goes away within a few minutes of stopping. Never at rest. No chronic cough, no wheeze, no phlegm. No fevers, no leg swelling, no palpitations, no fainting. Has never smoked anything. No dusty hobbies, no fumes at work. Weekend drinking about the same.

Father had emphysema diagnosed in his early 40s.

O: Thin, comfortable at rest, speaking in full sentences. Breath sounds a little distant with a long expiratory phase, no wheeze or crackles. Heart regular, no murmur, no gallop. No clubbing, no edema. ECG in office: normal sinus rhythm, no ST changes.

A/P
1. Exertional dyspnea, progressive, in a 30-year-old never smoker with a prolonged expiratory phase and a father with early emphysema. Needs lung testing. Referred to pulmonology for full PFTs and evaluation; I'd like them to look at alpha-1 given the family story. Rescue inhaler deferred until they see him.
2. Exercise-induced chest discomfort: brief, exertional, resolves with rest. ECG normal. Will see what the lung workup shows.
3. Alcohol use disorder: still drinking heavily on weekends, not ready to change. Brief counseling.
RTC after pulm.

reports.text: PA and lateral views. The lungs are hyperinflated with flattened hemidiaphragms. There is hyperlucency in both lower lobes. No focal consolidation, effusion or pneumothorax. Heart size normal. Mediastinal contours normal. Bones unremarkable.
reports.conclusion: Hyperinflation with bilateral lower lobe hyperlucency, consistent with emphysema.

reports.text: Spirometry, lung volumes by plethysmography, pre and post bronchodilator. Good effort and reproducibility. Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.46. FEV1 58% predicted. TLC 126% predicted. RV 172% predicted.
reports.conclusion: Obstructive ventilatory defect with hyperinflation and air trapping.

reports.text: Noncontrast CT of the chest. Panlobular emphysema, predominantly in the lower lobes bilaterally. No pulmonary nodule or mass. No interstitial abnormality. No bronchiectasis. Airways patent. No lymphadenopathy. No pleural or pericardial effusion. Upper abdomen unremarkable.
reports.conclusion: Lower-lobe-predominant panlobular emphysema. No nodule, mass or interstitial lung disease.

documents.title: Pulmonology Consultation
documents.author: pulmonology
documents.body:
Outside pulmonary practice. Date of consultation: 07/10/2023. Received by fax 08/14/2023.

Reason for consultation: progressive exertional dyspnea, requested by his primary care physician.

History: 30-year-old schoolteacher with about a year of worsening breathlessness and fatigue with aerobic exercise. He used to cycle to work and stopped recently because of it. Denies chronic cough, wheezing or sputum. Lifelong nonsmoker, does not use recreational drugs by his account, no occupational exposure to dusts, fumes or chemicals. Medications: none. Allergies: NKDA.

Family history: father with emphysema at 42 (former smoker); mother with cirrhosis of unknown cause.

Examination: thin young man, mildly tachypneic at rest. Increased AP diameter with a hyperexpanded chest. Breath sounds diminished throughout with prolonged expiration; no wheezes or crackles. Heart regular. No clubbing or edema.

Studies today: chest radiograph with hyperinflation, flat diaphragms and lower-lobe lucency. Full PFTs: post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.46, FEV1 58% predicted, TLC 126%, RV 172%. Noncontrast chest CT: lower-lobe-predominant panlobular emphysema without nodule, mass or interstitial change.

Impression: obstructive lung disease from basilar panlobular emphysema in a young never smoker, strongly suggestive of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Serum level and phenotype sent.

Plan:
- Start tiotropium 18 mcg inhaled once daily.
- Albuterol HFA 90 mcg, 2 puffs every 4-6 hours as needed for breathlessness.
- If deficiency is confirmed, we will begin weekly IV augmentation therapy and coordinate infusions.
- Strict avoidance of smoke exposure. Alcohol reduction advised given the liver risk if this proves to be AATD; recommend liver evaluation through primary care.
- Pneumococcal and annual influenza vaccination.

Addendum 07/24/2023: Alpha-1 antitrypsin 19 mg/dL (ref 100-190). Phenotype PiZZ. Diagnosis: alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, PiZZ, with panacinar emphysema. Discussed by phone with the patient; first-degree relatives should be offered testing. Augmentation therapy, Prolastin-C 60 mg/kg IV weekly, being arranged through specialty pharmacy.

documents.title: Pulmonology records

documents.body: Pt called. Says the lung specialist told him he has alpha-1 and wanted to know if we'd heard. Nothing received from pulmonology yet. Told him PCP will review once it arrives.

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Annual visit, also first visit since pulmonology.

Interval: Pulm consult 7/10 (letter reviewed): PFTs with FEV1/FVC 0.46, FEV1 58% pred, hyperinflation; CT with lower-lobe panlobular emphysema; AAT 19, phenotype ZZ. Dx alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency with panacinar emphysema. He is on tiotropium daily and albuterol as needed, using the rescue inhaler maybe twice a week with exertion. He tells me weekly infusions started at home three weeks ago with a visiting nurse, through pulmonology. Breathing a bit better on the daily inhaler; still not cycling.

Family: his sister got tested after his diagnosis and is a carrier (MZ). Parents not tested yet; he's going to raise it with his mother, given her cirrhosis.

Alcohol: still most weekends, 6-10 drinks a night. AUDIT-C 8. We spent time on why this matters more now: ZZ carries its own risk of liver disease, and alcohol adds to it. He heard me and says he'll cut back. Declines referral again.

Exam: thin. Mildly prolonged expiration, no wheeze. Heart RRR. Abdomen soft, no hepatosplenomegaly. No jaundice. No clubbing.

A/P
1. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, PiZZ, with panacinar emphysema: added to problem list. Inhalers reconciled. Augmentation per pulmonology. PCV20 today.
2. Liver evaluation for ZZ: hepatic panel and GGT today; RUQ ultrasound ordered.
3. Alcohol use disorder: counseled as above.
4. Exercise-induced chest discomfort: he hasn't noticed it since stopping the bike.
5. Vaccines: flu, updated COVID, PCV20 today.
RTC 6 months or after ultrasound if anything abnormal.

reports.text: Liver measures 14.6 cm in craniocaudal length with normal homogeneous echotexture and smooth contour. No focal hepatic lesion. Hepatic and portal veins patent with normal flow direction. Gallbladder without stones or wall thickening. Common bile duct 3 mm. Spleen normal in size at 10.2 cm. No ascites.
reports.conclusion: Normal liver and spleen. No sonographic evidence of chronic liver disease.

documents.title: Ultrasound and blood tests
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Eli, the liver ultrasound looks normal, no scarring or other changes, and your liver blood tests from the physical were normal too. That's good news. We'll keep checking yearly given the alpha-1, and keeping alcohol down is the best thing you can do for it.

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Emergency department record from an area hospital. Date of service 04/03/2024. Received by fax 04/25/2024.

Arrival by ambulance, early morning. Passerby found him asleep and hard to rouse on a park bench; he had been out drinking the night before and had slept with his right arm hooked over the back of the bench for several hours. Awake and conversant on arrival, smelling of alcohol, oriented.

PMH: alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (ZZ) with emphysema, followed by pulmonology. Home meds: tiotropium inhaled daily, albuterol inhaler as needed, Prolastin-C IV weekly. NKDA.

Exam: right wrist and fingers cannot extend against gravity, hand hangs in flexion. Decreased light touch over the back of the forearm and back of the hand, worst in the first web space. Triceps reflex present and symmetric; elbow extension strong. Grip limited by wrist position. Elbow and wrist without swelling, deformity, bruising or tenderness. No signs of head injury. Lungs: prolonged expiration, no wheeze.

Results: blood alcohol 241 mg/dL. Basic chemistry unremarkable.

Impression: 1) Acute alcohol intoxication. 2) Compressive right radial nerve palsy (prolonged pressure on the upper arm).

Plan: observed until clinically sober. Volar wrist cock-up splint applied. Expect gradual recovery; follow up with primary care this week. Counseled on alcohol. Discharged ambulatory.

documents.title: Right hand weakness after ED visit
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Pt calling from home. Was in an ER yesterday, woke up after a night out with his right hand "dead" and can't lift the wrist. They put him in a splint and told him to follow up with us. Numb on the back of the hand. No neck pain, no face or leg symptoms, no new weakness elsewhere, speaking normally. He is right handed and worried about teaching. Booked with PCP Monday 4/8. ED records not here; asked pt which hospital and will request.

medications.sig: 60 mg/kg IV infusion once weekly (home infusion, per pulmonology)

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Office Visit: ED Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: ER visit 4/3 (records requested, not yet received; history from pt). Out drinking Tuesday night after a colleague's farewell, doesn't remember much after midnight, woke on a park bench with his right arm over the back of it. Since then can't lift the right wrist or straighten the fingers; back of the hand numb, especially between thumb and index. Slightly better since Friday: he can now lift the fingers a little. No neck pain. Wearing the splint. Typing and writing on the whiteboard left-handed. Took two personal days.

He acknowledges this was a scary one. Drinks most weekends, last weekend 10+. AUDIT-C 9. Still says no drugs.

Meds reviewed: tiotropium daily, albuterol PRN, and weekly Prolastin-C home infusions since September (adding to our list now). Breathing stable.

O: Right wrist extension 2/5, finger extension at the MCPs 2/5, thumb extension weak. Elbow extension 5/5, triceps reflex 2+ and symmetric. Grip good with wrist passively supported. Sensation decreased over the dorsal radial hand and first web space. No elbow or wrist tenderness or swelling. Left arm normal.

A/P
1. Compressive radial nerve palsy, right: pattern fits compression at the upper arm with triceps spared. Already showing early return. Keep the cock-up splint for daytime use, gentle range of motion to keep the fingers from stiffening. Expect recovery over weeks to a few months; if no steady improvement by 6 weeks, would get nerve studies.
2. Acute alcohol intoxication, resolved. Alcohol use disorder: this event plus the pattern. Long talk. Offered referral to a counselor or addiction program and medication for cravings. He declines both for now but agreed to no drinking during recovery. Will keep asking.
3. AATD on augmentation: reconciled.
RTC 3 months, sooner if not improving.

documents.title: Office Visit: Right Arm Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Wrist and fingers came back over May; strength feels normal now and the numbness on the back of the hand is gone. Stopped the splint in early June. Since late in the school year, though, a deep ache in the top of the right forearm just below the elbow, worse after a day of writing on the board and carrying a bag of lab materials, better with rest. No numbness, no weakness. Pain 4/10 at worst.

Alcohol: says he stayed dry for about six weeks after April, back to weekends now but "less".

ED record from April arrived 4/25 and matches his account; blood alcohol was 241.

O: Full strength of wrist and finger extension, thumb extension and grip. Sensation intact throughout the hand. Tender over the extensor mass about 4 cm distal to the lateral epicondyle, not at the epicondyle itself. Pain reproduced with resisted forearm supination and with resisted middle finger extension. Elbow full range. Neck exam normal.

A/P
1. Radial nerve palsy, right: resolved.
2. Radial tunnel syndrome, right upper extremity: point tenderness over the radial tunnel with positive resisted supination and middle finger tests, no motor or sensory deficit. Relative rest, avoid sustained forearm rotation, stretch. Ibuprofen 400 mg with food as needed; keep to a few days a week, never on drinking days. Return if weakness.
3. Alcohol use disorder: affirmed the dry stretch. Still declines help.
Next: physical in October.

Outside pulmonary practice. Visit 08/12/2024. Received 08/26/2024.

Follow-up of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, ZZ, with panacinar emphysema. Receiving Prolastin-C 60 mg/kg IV weekly at home since September 2023, missing few doses, no infusion reactions. Uses tiotropium daily, albuterol about twice a week with exertion. No exacerbations this year. Had a right radial nerve injury in the spring that has recovered.

Exam: thin, no distress, prolonged expiration, no wheeze. No edema.

Spirometry: FEV1 56% predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.45, essentially stable from last year.

Assessment and plan: stable. Continue weekly augmentation, tiotropium and albuterol. Continue to avoid smoke. Reiterated alcohol reduction given liver risk. Annual influenza vaccine. Will submit renewal of the augmentation authorization. Return in one year with spirometry.

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Emergency department record from a regional medical center. Date of service 06/30/2025. Received 07/03/2025.

CC: chest discomfort, agitation and anxiety.

HPI: 32-year-old man with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (ZZ) brought in by friends from a party. They say he had been drinking and took something earlier in the night; he then became restless, chatty and elated. For the last hour he has felt keyed up, with waves of intense anxiety between bursts of energy, and complains of discomfort in his chest. No hallucinations. Pacing the room, talking fast. Patient says he only drank.

PMH: AATD with emphysema; right radial nerve injury 2024, followed for radial tunnel pain. Meds: tiotropium, albuterol PRN, weekly Prolastin-C, ibuprofen PRN. NKDA.

Triage: T 38.1 C, BP 168/96, HR 128, RR 24.

Exam: diaphoretic, pupils markedly dilated. Tachycardic, regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. Moving all extremities, no focal deficit.

ECG: sinus tachycardia, no acute ischemic changes. hs-troponin I within normal limits. Urine drug screen positive for cocaine. Chemistry unremarkable.

Course: lorazepam 2 mg IV given with good effect; calmer, heart rate and pressure came down, chest discomfort resolved. Observed several hours.

Diagnosis: cocaine intoxication; alcohol use.

Disposition: discharged early morning with friend. Counseled about cocaine and chest pain risk; resources for substance use given. Follow up with PCP within one week.

conditions.label: Cocaine use disorder
conditions.note: Patient denies use; positive ED urine screen

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Office Visit: ED Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: ER 6/30 (record received 7/3, reviewed). At a party, drank, then got wired, anxious, chest felt tight; friends brought him in. ER found temp 38.1, BP 168/96, HR 128, dilated pupils, sweating; ECG sinus tach, troponin normal, urine screen positive for cocaine; settled with IV lorazepam. He feels completely fine since. No chest discomfort at rest or with walking. Breathing at baseline.

I went over the urine result with him. He says he did not take cocaine and thinks someone must have slipped something into a drink. Not upset with the question, just firm. Drinking: weekends, a lot at that party. AUDIT-C 8.

O: calm, well appearing. BP and pulse normal today. Pupils equal, normal size. Heart RRR no murmur. Lungs prolonged expiration, no wheeze. No tremor.

A/P
1. Cocaine intoxication 6/30, resolved. Cocaine use disorder, recorded on the basis of the toxicology and presentation; he denies use. Explained plainly what cocaine does to heart rhythm and blood pressure, and with his lungs, why it worries me. Offered addiction medicine referral, which can be confidential and outside of school; he declines. Will keep it open.
2. Alcohol use disorder: ongoing. Counseled again; declines medication or counseling.
3. AATD with emphysema: stable, continue regimen.
4. Exercise-induced chest discomfort: not recurring with his current activity.
Physical in October.

documents.title: Office Visit: Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Spring follow-up.

Lungs: no change in what he can do; walks most places, still not back on the bike. Weekly infusions ongoing. Tiotropium daily, albuterol 1-2 times a week. No exacerbations. Says he did not get to pulmonology last year and has a visit with them this summer.

Forearm: flares after report-card week, ibuprofen a few times, settles.

Alcohol: says he has cut back, a few drinks on a weekend night, a couple of dry weekends this spring. AUDIT-C 6. Denies cocaine or other drugs.

Exam: thin, comfortable. Prolonged expiration, no wheeze or crackles. Heart RRR. Abdomen soft, no hepatomegaly. Right forearm minimal tenderness, normal strength.

A/P
1. AATD with panacinar emphysema: stable. Continue tiotropium, albuterol, augmentation per pulm; glad he has a pulm visit set.
2. Liver monitoring: hepatic panel and GGT, plus CBC today.
3. Alcohol use disorder: real improvement by his report; encouraged. Cocaine use disorder: denies; offer of help stands.
4. Radial tunnel syndrome, right: stable.
Physical booked for October with flu and COVID vaccines.

documents.title: Emergency Department Observation Summary
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Emergency department and observation summary, area hospital. Dates 07/05/2026 to 07/06/2026. Received by fax 08/19/2026.

Presentation: 33-year-old man with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (ZZ) and panacinar emphysema, brought by friends after he collapsed at a nightclub, confused, hyperactive and talking rapidly. Friends report hours of drinking, unusual energy and nonstop talking, with repeated trips to the bathroom after which he seemed recharged. They also mention he sometimes gets chest discomfort when exercising. A similar ED visit last summer is in our records.

PMH: AATD with emphysema, alcohol use disorder, cocaine intoxication 2025, radial tunnel syndrome right. Meds: tiotropium, albuterol, Prolastin-C weekly IV, ibuprofen PRN. NKDA.

Arrival: BP 188/102, HR 132, RR 24. Diaphoretic, very agitated and combative, pupils widely dilated, mucous membranes dry. Limited neuro exam without focal findings. Monitor showed frequent PVCs; he grabbed his chest describing severe substernal pain.

Course: lorazepam 2 mg IV with improvement in agitation, then heart rate and blood pressure. ECG sinus tachycardia with frequent PVCs, no ST elevation. hs-troponin I normal at arrival and at 3 hours. Urine drug screen positive for cocaine. Chemistry unremarkable. Chest pain resolved; PVCs settled on monitoring overnight.

Diagnoses: cocaine intoxication with chest pain; alcohol intoxication.

Disposition: discharged home 07/06 morning, alert and calm. Advised to avoid cocaine and alcohol; addiction treatment resources given. Follow up with primary care.

documents.title: ER over the weekend
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Just so you know, I ended up in the ER Saturday night into Sunday. Heart racing and chest pain, they kept me overnight and said my heart was fine. Feeling ok now. Can it wait until my physical?

documents.title: RE: ER over the weekend
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Thanks for telling me, Eli. I'm glad you're feeling better. I haven't received anything from the hospital yet; we'll request the records. I'd rather see you before October to go over what happened. Front desk can find a summer slot, or a video visit works. Any chest pain, fainting or a racing heart again, go straight to the ER.

documents.title: RE: ER over the weekend
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Ok. I'm away visiting family most of July, I'll just keep the October one if that's alright.
